lessons.title: Recognizing Good vs Spoiled Silage by Smell and Texture
lessons.body:
Good silage smells like sweet vinegar or fresh bread. It has a sharp, pleasant tang that tickles your nose. When you squeeze a handful, it feels like a wrung-out spongeâmoist but not dripping. The colour is usually light green to yellowish-green, like tobacco. If you open a pit and get a whiff of alcohol or nail polish remover, that's a sign of yeast or clostridia. Spoiled silage smells like rancid butter, manure, or rotten eggs. That foul smell comes from butyric acid or putrefying proteins. Never feed this to animals.

Texture tells you a lot. Grab a fistful from 15 cm inside the silage face. Good silage holds together but breaks apart easily when you rub it. It should not be slimy or sticky. If it feels like wet sawdust, it was too dry and likely heated. If it drips brown liquid, it's too wet and probably has butyric acid. In Africa, where humidity and heat vary, always test the top 30 cm and the bottom 30 cm separatelyâspoilage often starts at the edges.

Smell test: take a sample in a bucket, step away from the pit, and sniff. If you can smell it on your clothes after 5 minutes, it's bad. Good silage smell fades quickly. For texture, squeeze a handful hard. If water runs out, it's too wet. If it crumbles and dust flies, it's too dry. Aim for 30-35% dry matter. You can estimate: a soccer-ball-sized sample should weigh about 1.5 kg when wet. If it weighs less than 1 kg, it's too dry.

In tropical heat, silage can spoil within 24 hours of opening if not fed fast. Always remove at least 10 cm from the face daily. If you see white or grey mould, that's yeast and mouldânot always deadly but reduces quality. Black or green mould means Aspergillus or Penicillium, which can produce toxins. Discard any mouldy layer. Trust your senses: if it smells like a swamp or a brewery, don't feed it. Good silage makes cows lick the trough; bad silage makes them turn away.

lessons.title: Identifying Mould, Yeast, and Butyric Acid Problems
lessons.body:
Mould appears as fuzzy patchesâwhite, grey, green, or black. White mould is often harmless yeast, but green or black mould means mycotoxins. In Africa, Aspergillus flavus produces aflatoxin, which can kill livestock and contaminate milk. If you see mould on more than 10% of the silage face, discard the whole top layer. Yeast looks like a white, powdery film and smells like beer or bread. Yeast causes heating when silage is exposed to air. A silage that smells like a brewery has yeast overgrowthâfeed it quickly or it will turn mouldy.

Butyric acid smells like rancid butter or vomit. It comes from Clostridium bacteria that grow when silage is too wet (below 25% dry matter) and too cold or too hot. In Africa, this often happens in poorly compacted pits during rainy season. Butyric silage has a slimy texture and a yellowish-brown colour. It can cause ketosis in dairy cows and reduce milk production by up to 30%. Never feed butyric silage to pregnant animalsâit can cause abortions.

To test for butyric acid, take 100 g of silage, add 200 ml of warm water, and stir. Smell the water. If it smells like rancid butter, it's butyric. Another sign: the silage pH is above 5.0. You can buy pH strips cheaply at farm supply shops. Good silage has pH 3.8â4.5. If pH is 5.5 or higher, butyric bacteria are active. Also check for slime: rub a handful between your fingers. If it feels soapy, that's butyric.

Prevention is better than cure. Wilt forage to 30-35% dry matter before ensiling. Add molasses (5 kg per tonne) or lactic acid bacteria inoculant to speed fermentation. Compact well to remove air. Cover with a plastic sheet and weigh it down with tyres or soil. In hot climates, open pits only in the cool morning. If you find mould, cut out 30 cm around it and feed the rest immediately. If butyric acid is present, do not feedâdispose of it safely (see Lesson 6).

lessons.title: Preventing Heating and Spoilage in Hay Stacks
lessons.body:
Heating in hay stacks happens when moisture is above 20%. Bacteria and fungi multiply, raising the temperature. At 40Â°C, hay starts to brown and lose protein. At 60Â°C, it can spontaneously combust. In Africa, where daytime temperatures reach 35Â°C, hay must be dried to 15% moisture or less before stacking. Test by twisting a handful: if it snaps and breaks, it's dry enough. If it feels rubbery, dry it longer.

Build stacks on a raised platformâpallets or stonesâto keep off the ground. Use a layer of dry straw or plastic at the bottom. Stack in a pyramid shape, not a cube, so air can circulate. Leave 30 cm gaps between stacks. In humid regions, add a roof of thatch or tarpaulin. Never stack hay directly against a wall. If you stack in a barn, leave 1 m between the stack and the wall. For small bales, stack them on their edges, not flat, to allow airflow.

Monitor temperature daily for the first two weeks. Push a metal rod (like a crowbar) into the centre of the stack. Leave it for 20 minutes, then pull it out. If it's too hot to hold, the hay is heating. If the rod is too hot to touch, move the hay immediatelyâspread it out to cool. A simple thermometer probe (available at agricultural stores) can be inserted 1 m deep. If temperature exceeds 50Â°C, tear down the stack. If it's 60Â°C or more, call for helpâfire risk is high.

Prevent heating by using salt. Sprinkle 1 kg of coarse salt per 100 kg of hay as you stack. Salt absorbs moisture and inhibits bacteria. Alternatively, use propionic acid (commercial hay preservative) at 1% of dry weight. In Africa, many farmers use wood ashâit's alkaline and reduces mould. But ash can reduce palatability. Best practice: dry thoroughly, stack loosely, and check temperature daily. If you see steam rising from the stack in the morning, it's heating. Act fast: spread the hay in the sun for a day, then restack.

lessons.title: Testing Hay Quality with Simple Hand Tests
lessons.body:
You don't need a lab to judge hay. Start with your eyes. Good hay is green, leafy, and smells sweet like tea. Brown or yellow hay was rained on or stored too long. Black hay is mouldyâdon't feed it. Look for dust: shake a handful. If dust flies, it's mouldy or too dry. In Africa, where many farmers make hay from Napier grass or maize stover, colour matters: Napier hay should be light green; maize stover is naturally pale but should not be grey.

Smell test: grab a big handful and sniff. Fresh hay smells like dried grass. If it smells like tobacco or caramel, it heated. If it smells like mildew or mushrooms, it's mouldy. If it smells like nothing, it's old and low in nutrients. For a more precise test, put a sample in a sealed jar for 30 minutes. Open it and smell. A strong off-smell means poor quality.

Texture test: take a handful and rub it between your palms. Good hay is soft and pliable. Stems should break easily but not shatter. If it's prickly and sharp, it was cut too lateâanimals will waste it. If it's brittle and crumbles, it's too dry. For a moisture test, twist a small handful tightly. If it springs back and feels cool, moisture is about 15%âperfect. If it stays twisted and feels damp, moisture is above 20%âdry it more. If it cracks and breaks, moisture is below 10%âtoo dry, but still safe.

A simple density test: grab a handful and squeeze. Good hay should feel like a spongeâspringy but not hard. If it feels like a brick, it was compressed too much and may heat. If it feels like cotton, it's too loose and will spoil. For a quick protein estimate, look at the leaves. Leaves have more protein than stems. If you see more than 50% leaves, it's good quality. For maize stover, leaves are the most nutritious part. Finally, a taste test: chew a small piece. Sweet hay is high in sugar and palatable. Bitter or sour hay is spoiled. Never swallowâjust taste and spit.

lessons.title: Fixing Common Silage Fermentation Failures
lessons.body:
Failure 1: Silage smells like vinegar but is slimy. This means too much acetic acid and not enough lactic acid. Cause: too wet (below 25% dry matter) or too cold. Fix: next time, wilt longer to 30-35% dry matter. Add molasses (5 kg per tonne) to feed lactic bacteria. If the silage is already made, mix it with dry hay (1 part silage to 1 part hay) to absorb moisture and improve fermentation. Feed within 2 weeks.

Failure 2: Silage smells like alcohol or nail polish. This is yeast overgrowth. Cause: air exposure during storage or feeding. Fix: compact better and seal the pit with a double layer of plastic. If you see white yeast on the face, remove 15 cm and feed the rest quickly. Add a lactic acid bacteria inoculant next time. For existing silage, mix with 2% salt to inhibit yeast.

Failure 3: Silage is black and slimy. This is clostridial fermentation (butyric acid). Cause: too wet and too much soil contamination. Fix: never ensile wet forage. Wilt to 35% dry matter. Add 1% salt or 5 kg molasses per tonne. If black slime is present, do not feedâdispose of it. For the rest of the pit, if only the top 20 cm is black, remove it and feed the good silage below.

Failure 4: Silage is dry and mouldy. Cause: too dry (above 40% dry matter) and poor compaction. Fix: chop finer (2-3 cm) and add water if needed. For existing silage, rehydrate by mixing with wet brewers' grain or fresh grass. But if mould is green or black, discard.

Failure 5: Silage pH is above 5.0. This means fermentation stalled. Cause: low sugar content or cold weather. Fix: add molasses or ground maize (10 kg per tonne) at ensiling. For existing silage, mix with 5% molasses solution and repack. If pH remains high after 2 weeks, feed only to beef cattle, not dairy.

General fix: always test pH with strips. Good silage pH is 3.8-4.5. If pH is 4.6-5.0, feed within 1 week. If above 5.0, treat as spoiled. In Africa, where temperatures fluctuate, use a thermometer to check internal temperature. If above 35Â°C, repack and seal. Remember: the best fix is preventionâwilt, chop, compact, and seal.

lessons.title: Safe Disposal of Spoiled Fodder
lessons.body:
Spoiled fodder contains mycotoxins, butyric acid, and harmful bacteria. Never feed it to any animal, not even pigs or chickens. It can cause abortions, reduced milk, and death. Do not dump it in the animal penâanimals will eat it. Do not put it in the compost heap if it has black mould, because spores can spread. The safest method is deep burial. Dig a pit at least 1 metre deep, far from water sources (at least 30 metres from wells or streams). Place the spoiled fodder in the pit and cover with 30 cm of soil. Add lime (1 kg per 100 kg of fodder) to speed decomposition and reduce smell. Tamp down the soil.

Another option is burning. But burning mouldy hay releases toxic spores into the air. If you must burn, do it on a windless day, far from houses and animal sheds. Wear a mask (N95 or cloth soaked in water). Burn in a metal drum or a shallow pit. After burning, bury the ash. Never burn plastic twine or net wrapâit releases dioxins. In Africa, many farmers burn crop residues, but spoiled silage is differentâit's wet and won't burn well. So burial is better.

For small amounts (less than 50 kg), you can use a sealed plastic bag. Put the spoiled fodder in a heavy-duty bag, add 500 g of lime, tie it tightly, and leave it in the sun for 2 weeks. The heat and lime will kill most pathogens. Then bury the bag. Do not open it indoors. For liquid runoff from spoiled silage, dig a small catchment pit and add lime. Never let runoff flow into rivers or pondsâit kills fish.

After disposal, clean all tools and boots with a 10% bleach solution (1 part bleach to 9 parts water). Wash your hands with soap. Change clothes. If you feel dizzy or nauseous after handling mouldy fodder, see a health workerâmycotoxins can affect humans too. Prevention is cheaper than disposal: make good silage and hay so you never have to bury it. But when spoilage happens, act fast and safely. Never sell spoiled fodderâit's illegal and unethical.

quiz.q: What does good silage smell like?
options: B) Sweet vinegar or fresh bread
quiz.explanation: Good silage has a pleasant, tangy smell from lactic acid fermentation.

quiz.q: What is the ideal dry matter content for silage?
quiz.explanation: 30-35% dry matter allows proper fermentation and prevents butyric acid.

quiz.q: What does a slimy texture in silage indicate?
quiz.explanation: Slimy silage is a sign of butyric acid bacteria or yeast overgrowth.

quiz.q: Which mould colour is most dangerous due to mycotoxins?
quiz.explanation: Green and black moulds like Aspergillus produce aflatoxins.

quiz.q: What does butyric acid smell like?
quiz.explanation: Butyric acid has a distinct rancid butter smell.

quiz.q: What pH range indicates good silage?
quiz.explanation: Good silage has a pH between 3.8 and 4.5 due to lactic acid.

quiz.q: How much molasses should you add per tonne of silage to improve fermentation?
quiz.explanation: 5 kg of molasses per tonne provides sugars for lactic acid bacteria.

quiz.q: What causes heating in hay stacks?
quiz.explanation: Moisture above 20% allows bacteria and fungi to multiply and generate heat.

quiz.q: At what temperature should you tear down a hay stack?
quiz.explanation: At 50Â°C, heating is dangerous and can lead to spontaneous combustion.

quiz.q: How much salt can you sprinkle per 100 kg of hay to prevent heating?
quiz.explanation: 1 kg of coarse salt per 100 kg of hay absorbs moisture and inhibits bacteria.

quiz.q: What is a sign of good hay colour?
quiz.explanation: Green hay indicates good drying and nutrient retention.

quiz.q: What does a sweet taste in hay indicate?
quiz.explanation: Sweet hay is high in sugars and is more palatable to animals.

quiz.q: How can you test hay moisture with a hand twist?
options: A) If it springs back, moisture is 15%
B) If it stays twisted, moisture is 15%
C) If it crumbles, moisture is 20%
D) If it drips, moisture is 10%
quiz.explanation: Hay that springs back after twisting has about 15% moisture, ideal for storage.

quiz.q: What does a prickly, sharp texture in hay indicate?
quiz.explanation: Late-cut hay has tough, sharp stems that animals waste.

quiz.q: What is the first sign of silage fermentation failure?
options: B) Off-smell like vinegar or alcohol
quiz.explanation: Off-smells indicate wrong bacteria or yeast are active.

quiz.q: What causes silage to smell like alcohol?
quiz.explanation: Yeast produces alcohol and causes heating when exposed to air.

quiz.q: How can you fix silage that is too wet and slimy?
quiz.explanation: Mixing with dry hay absorbs moisture and improves fermentation.

quiz.q: What should you do if silage pH is above 5.0?
quiz.explanation: pH above 5.0 means fermentation failed and spoilage bacteria are active.

quiz.q: What is the safest way to dispose of spoiled fodder?
quiz.explanation: Deep burial prevents animals and humans fromæ¥è§¦ toxins.

quiz.q: How deep should you dig a pit for spoiled fodder?
quiz.explanation: A 1-metre deep pit ensures animals cannot dig it up.

quiz.q: How far should the disposal pit be from water sources?
quiz.explanation: 30 metres prevents contamination of wells and streams.

quiz.q: What can you add to spoiled fodder in a pit to reduce smell and speed decomposition?
quiz.explanation: Lime raises pH and inhibits pathogens.

quiz.q: Why is burning mouldy hay dangerous?
quiz.explanation: Burning releases mycotoxin-laden spores into the air.

quiz.q: What should you wear when handling spoiled fodder?
quiz.explanation: A mask and gloves protect against spores and bacteria.

quiz.q: What is the first step to prevent silage fermentation failures?
quiz.explanation: Proper wilting ensures good fermentation and prevents butyric acid.

quiz.q: What does a soapy feel when rubbing silage indicate?
quiz.explanation: Butyric acid feels soapy and smells rancid.

quiz.q: How often should you check hay stack temperature?
options: B) Daily for first two weeks
quiz.explanation: Heating can occur quickly, so daily checks are critical early on.

quiz.q: What tool can you use to check hay stack temperature?
quiz.explanation: A metal rod conducts heat and can be felt by hand.

quiz.q: What is a sign of good hay texture?
quiz.explanation: Soft, pliable hay is palatable and easy to digest.

quiz.q: What should you do after disposing of spoiled fodder?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning with bleach prevents spread of pathogens.
